title: Sitting in check while the partner mates first
summary: Queens and rooks cross the boards all game. Black on board A gets far ahead by its own count, then gives up its queen, and a queen taken on board B turns board A into a mating attack for White. Facing mate there, Black on board A sits in check, and its partner mates first with N@e5# on board B.
event: HypeBeast 1.1.1 against HypeBeast 1.1.0, 500,000 nodes a move

result.text: White on board B mates; the team of A-Black and B-White wins.

moves.note: The first sacrifice of the game. Kxf7 sends this bishop to White on board B, who drops it as B@f3 at move 10. On board B, Nxc3 at once hands White here a knight, dropped next move as N@d3.
White takes Black's queen. It goes to its partner on board B, who drops it as Q@a5 at move 18.

Black takes on c3 while its queen on d7 can be won by N@f6+ gxf6 Nxf6+. Its own line shows exactly that, and it still liked the move because it counted the two knights it would capture as worth a lot to its partner on board A. White played the line, and by its next move Black scored itself nearly ten pawns down. The first of those knights went across at once and came down as N@g5+.

lines.note: Its own line: White wins the queen with the knight sacrifice on f6 and Nxd7.
A search that ignores the other board moves the queen first with Qd8; searched the same way, it scored much better for Black than bxc3.
White's own plan at its next move, the same sacrifice, which it scored about seven pawns in its favour.

moves.note: White on board B has just taken that queen with Qxa5, so Black here holds two queens, and it drops one on g6. Its first choice was B@f7; it switched because Q@g6 did better in case a knight came to it or a pawn to White, and a knight did come, from Bxc6. By its own count Black was now about ten pawns ahead on this board.

Its first choice was Rxa1. It thought Black would probably get a knight from board A soon, and with a knight in Black's hand it rated Bxc6 clearly better. No knight came. Black answered Rxb1+, and that rook went to White on board A, who dropped it at once with R@f7+; Qxf7 took it there and sent it back to this board.

lines.note: Black's best answer by a fresh search, exactly what followed in the game, scored well in White's favour.
The first choice, taking the rook on a1.

moves.note: By its own count White was about 30 pawns down, and most of that was the danger to its partner on board B: it rated any knight, bishop, rook or queen that Black captured here as enough for White on board B to mate. Its line expects cxd6 and Bxf7 winning the queen. Black played Qxc4+ instead, giving up the queen for the bishop, and after Nxc4 that queen went to its partner on board B.

lines.note: The line it expected: Black takes back on d6 and White wins the queen with Bxf7.

moves.note: Black gives its queen for the bishop on c4, and after Nxc4 the queen goes to Black on board B. Black was well ahead here by its count; by its next move it scored this board about level. On board B that queen later blocks a check as Q@d8 and then takes White's queen with Qxc8, which goes to White on this board and comes down as Q@e6+.

Black here now has the queen from board A in hand. Its first choice was Q@e4+; it took the rook instead, nearly the same by its count, and the rook went to White on board A, who later dropped rooks on f8 and h8. This board, well in White's favour two moves earlier, was now about level by Black's count.

Its first choice was R@a8+. It thought Black would probably get a queen from board B soon, and with a queen in Black's hand it rated Rxe8+ better. The bishop taken on e8 went straight to its partner on board B, who dropped it at once with B@a6+.

lines.note: The first choice: R@a8+ and a trade on b8 before the same exchange on e8.
A search that ignores the other board drops a rook on d7; searched the same way, it scored about even, against about twelve pawns for White after Rxe8+.
With a queen added to Black's hand it still plays Rxe8+ and follows with R@a8+.

moves.note: Nearly forced: Kd7 scored far worse by its count. Black still scored itself slightly ahead, but White's next search already scored the board well in White's favour, and then White's partner on board B played Qxc8, sending a queen that came down here as Q@e6+. Black had not expected a queen to reach White. By its next move Black's own score had collapsed.

lines.note: Its own line: White checks with R@h8+ and B@h5+, and Black blocks each with a drop.
White's own plan at its next move, R@g8+ and Nd6+, which it scored about eight pawns in its favour.

moves.note: The pawn is what was left of a queen on board B: bxc8=Q+ promoted there, Bxc8 took the new queen, and a promoted piece crosses as a pawn. White was nearly sure it would come when it dropped Q@e6+. By its count P@d7+ forced mate in three, finishing with R@e8+ Bxe8 dxe8=Q+.

lines.note: A search that ignores the other board prefers P@f7+, also a forced mate, but a move slower by the same kind of search.

moves.note: Its first choice was R@e8+, mate in two by its count, but Bxe8 would hand that rook to White on board B, where it saw a rook drop on d8 as mate. So it chose R@h8+, a slower mate by its own count. White on board B already held a rook in hand, though, and the mate here never came: Black sat in check at the end while its partner mated on board B.

lines.note: Black's best defence by a fresh search: block with Q@g8, and White still mates.
The first choice: the fastest mate, but Bxe8 takes a rook for White on board B.

moves.note: The same worry again: its first choice Rxg8+ let Nxg8 take the rook, and White on board B could drop it as R@d8, mate there. N@d7+ first was only a move slower by its count. On its next move Rxg8+ took the rook on g8 for its own partner instead, who used it for R@e2+.

lines.note: Black's reply by a fresh search: Ke8, and White still mates.
The first choice, which lets Nxg8 win the rook.

moves.note: Takes the rook and leaves Black mated in two by its count; exf8=N+ and N@e5+ mated as well. Its partner on board A was lost by its own count, so it gave no value to anything sent across. The rook went to Black on board A, who never moved again.

lines.note: It expects c5 and N@e5+, the mate that came two moves later.

moves.note: Lost either way by its count. The rook had just come from board A, where its partner took on g8. The check only delays the mate, and Kxe2 sends the rook on to Black on board A, who was sitting.

lines.note: A search that ignores the other board checks from d1 instead, just as lost.

moves.note: Takes the rook; Bxe2 mated just as well by its count. Black has one move left before N@e5#.

Mate. On board A Black had been sitting in check since shortly after Rxg8+, every move there leading to mate by its count. Its partner here had mate in two and its clock was about a second and a half longer than Black's on this board, so it sat and let this mate land first.
